newsitem.title: USA: McDougal says he "tired of lying" for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: McDougal says he "tired of lying" for Clinton.

text.p: James McDougal, sentenced to three years in prison on Monday on Whitewater-related charges, said he was now cooperating with investigators because he was "sick and tired of lying" for President Bill Clinton.

In an interview with Dateline NBC, McDougal said he was providing fresh information in part because Clinton failed to extend a pardon to his ex-wife Susan McDougal, another player in the failed Whitewater real estate deal.
"I wasn't so much concerned that he'd abandoned me. I felt he'd abandoned Susan," McDougal said in the interview, which will be aired in full on Tuesday.
"I really thought he would pardon her -- that was a big factor in my decision," he said. "I just got sick and tired of lying for the fellow, you know."

McDougal, 56, had faced up to 81 years in prison for his conviction last May on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy, but got a lesser sentence because of his cooperation with Whitewater independent prosecutor Kenneth Starr.
In his NBC interview, McDougal again hinted he had given investigators information that could implicate the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton in the scandal.
"I think they should be deeply concerned," he said.
McDougal has reportedly told investigators that in 1986, as governor of Arkansas, Clinton was involved in an illegal $300,000 federally-backed loan -- a statement Clinton has denied under oath.

Susan McDougal, convicted with her former husband and sentenced to two years in prison for her role in the fraudulent loan schemes, has refused to cooperate with Starr and is currently serving a contempt of court sentence.
She has said James McDougal told her he was lying to win a reduced sentence and that he urged her to do the same.
McDougal told Dateline NBC he knew his personal credibility might be suspect, but he was confident his information would be corroborated.
McDougal has been the central figure of the Whitewater saga since it flared up in 1993 and was far closer to Clinton than anyone else brought to trial in the investigation.
He also said he felt no guilt in turning on the Clintons, who were once his good friends.
"I think the Clintons are really sort of like tornadoes moving through people's lives...I'm just one of the people left in the wake of their passing by," McDougal said.
"But I have no whining or complaining to do, because I have lots of company."
